registered.old: Under § 89 a modification of a contract not fully performed on either side binds if fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated when the contract was made, to the extent a statute provides (UCC § 2-209 and N.Y. Gen. Oblig. L. § 5-1103 remove the consideration requirement), or to the extent justice requires because of a material change of position in reliance. Modifications may also be enforced as waivers, but only until retracted unless relied on.
registered.new: Under § 89 a modification of a contract not fully performed on either side binds if fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated when the contract was made, to the extent a statute provides (UCC § 2-209 and N.Y. Gen. Oblig. L. § 5-1103 remove the consideration requirement), or to the extent justice requires because of a material change of position in reliance. Legal qualification: UCC § 2-209(1) removes the consideration requirement only for modifications of contracts within Article 2 (goods), and the modification must still meet the Code's test of good faith (comment 2); N.Y. Gen. Oblig. L. § 5-1103 applies only to a modification in writing signed by the party against whom it is enforced or by that party's agent. Modifications may also be enforced as waivers, but only until retracted unless relied on.

registered.old: Contractual limits on modification are ineffective (“Those who make a contract may unmake it”), but no-oral-modification clauses are made effective by statutes such as UCC § 2-209 and N.Y. Gen. Oblig. L. § 15-301, though they may be read narrowly in light of waiver and estoppel. Other tools are limits on agents' authority and commitments to transfer value to third parties if a modification occurs, such as most-favoured-nation clauses.

Gen. Oblig. L. § 15-301, though they may be read narrowly in light of waiver and estoppel. Legal qualification: under UCC § 2-209(2) the clause must be in a signed agreement, and, except as between merchants, a clause on a form supplied by a merchant binds the other party only if that party signs it separately. Other tools are limits on agents' authority and commitments to transfer value to third parties if a modification occurs, such as most-favoured-nation clauses.

registered.old: Duress requires an improper threat, which once meant unlawful confinement or bodily harm and now extends to property and economic harm, including breach of contract and a threat to breach the duty of good faith; the absence of a reasonable alternative; and unfair terms, which matter less if the threat is improper enough. A threat to breach “without legitimate commercial reason” can be a breach of the duty of good faith (UCC § 2-209, comment 2).
registered.new: Duress requires an improper threat, which once meant unlawful confinement or bodily harm and now extends to property and economic harm, including breach of contract and a threat to breach the duty of good faith; the absence of a reasonable alternative; and unfair terms, which matter less if the threat is improper enough. Legal qualification: Restatement § 175(1) does not list unfair terms as an element; they are required only for threats that are improper under § 176(2), while a threat listed in § 176(1), such as a threat to breach the duty of good faith and fair dealing, is improper whatever the terms. A threat to breach “without legitimate commercial reason” can be a breach of the duty of good faith (UCC § 2-209, comment 2).

registered.old: Slide 8's table maps Restatement and UCC § 2-202 terms. A partially integrated (“final”) writing discharges prior inconsistent agreements (§§ 213(1), 215) but can be supplemented by consistent additional terms (§ 216(1)). A completely integrated (“final, complete and exclusive”) writing also discharges prior consistent agreements within its scope (§ 213(2)) and cannot be supplemented by consistent additional terms within its scope; under UCC § 2-202(a), course of performance, course of dealing and usage of trade may still explain or supplement it. A merger clause is relevant to the extent of integration but not dispositive, and parol evidence can still challenge the validity of a completely integrated agreement.
registered.new: Slide 8's table maps Restatement and UCC § 2-202 terms. A partially integrated (“final”) writing discharges prior inconsistent agreements (§§ 213(1), 215) but can be supplemented by consistent additional terms (§ 216(1)). A completely integrated (“final, complete and exclusive”) writing also discharges prior consistent agreements within its scope (§ 213(2)) and cannot be supplemented by consistent additional terms within its scope; under UCC § 2-202(a), course of performance, course of dealing and usage of trade may still explain or supplement it. A merger clause is relevant to the extent of integration but not dispositive, and parol evidence can still challenge the validity of a completely integrated agreement. Legal qualification: courts are split on merger clauses. Some treat the clause as conclusive proof that the writing is completely integrated, while others treat it as strong but rebuttable evidence (C&M 542).
